Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ to the canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}.$
question.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=4, \quad$ $\lambda_2=2, \quad$ and $\quad\lambda_3=1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/3c63f40791eabbb3bf542c071457a85f5d905c35c4584fcf3cfe7d848b61651d.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/024e6e0876d7675e176c03019352b4ebcee57f8a0f70e0bc3f18b5f64358abab.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/a09d93da71b4cd0a3e486e3f86de9d57cae3d663aaa32e4b0a12c556e1e83c67.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/02fd6729a1ad101039782476c94b46c5edf05b40b2119fa9605eab4008f82ebd.svg)

- For $\lambda_3=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/b8895aec0d3901c5cdea3ef4da292741fe9ce4b015f619450da70673ab88c318.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_3  \| = 1,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14228498/assets/24aebe9839a5f13fb12ff18053f2c1537000af33af37429eae1a3c6110b3dc6a.svg)

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
